cp01-03.title: Gaius Marius is consul for the first time
cp01-03.place: Rome; the war in Numidia (Algeria and Tunisia)
paras: Gaius Marius came from Arpinum in Latium and was a 'new man' (novus homo), the first of his family in Roman high office. Plutarch says his parents were poor labourers, but Wikipedia judges this almost certainly false, as his family was locally important. Rome was then at war with Jugurtha, king of Numidia, whose bribes and early victories had shaken trust in the aristocracy's handling of the war. From 109 BC Marius served in Numidia as the senior officer of the consul Quintus Caecilius Metellus, his old patron. He fell out with Metellus, who mocked his wish to stand for consul, and won over the soldiers and the Italian traders in Africa by promising to end the war quickly.

Marius was elected consul for 107 BC. The Senate had extended Metellus's command, but a friendly tribune had the people's assembly transfer the Numidian war to Marius, and Metellus left Africa without meeting him. To fill his army Marius took volunteers, including men without property who had normally been kept out of the legions; Plutarch says this was against law and custom. His quaestor, who brought the cavalry, was Lucius Cornelius Sulla.

Jugurtha fought a guerrilla war, and the fighting lasted longer than Marius had promised. In 107 BC he won a battle near Cirta and took Capsa after a desert march. The war ended when King Bocchus of Mauretania, Jugurtha's father-in-law, handed Jugurtha over to Sulla. Jugurtha was led in Marius's triumph in 104 BC and died in prison. The quarrel over who deserved the credit began the enmity between Marius and Sulla. Marius went on to hold six more consulships, five of them in a row from 104 to 100 BC against the invading Cimbri and Teutones.

cp01-06.title: Sulla becomes dictator
paras: Lucius Cornelius Sulla won the civil war against the followers of Marius and Cinna at the Colline Gate outside Rome in November 82 BC. The next day, while he addressed the Senate in the temple of Bellona, thousands of captured Samnites were being butchered nearby. He then began the proscriptions: published lists of men who could be killed without trial, with rewards for their killers and informers, their property seized and sold, and their descendants barred from office. Appian says the first list named about 40 senators and 1,600 knights; Wikipedia says it had some 80 names, with hundreds more added in the following days. Many were listed so that Sulla's partisans could settle scores or buy their property cheaply at auction.

Both consuls of 82 BC were dead, Carbo executed and the younger Marius a suicide at Praeneste. Sulla had the Senate choose an interrex, the aged Lucius Valerius Flaccus, who put a law to the people (the lex Valeria) making Sulla dictator 'for writing laws and setting the state in order'. Unlike the old emergency dictatorship, an office unused since the Second Punic War, the appointment had no time limit, and it covered everything Sulla had done or would do. Appian calls the result a kingship or tyranny in all but name.

As dictator Sulla tried to secure the Senate's rule. Tribunes of the plebs lost the right to propose laws and were barred from higher office. He increased the numbers of praetors and quaestors, made former quaestors members of the Senate, and added about 300 knights to the thinned Senate. He expanded the permanent criminal courts and staffed them with senators, and required ten years before a man could hold the same office again. He freed more than 10,000 slaves of the proscribed, who took his family name of Cornelius, and settled his veterans on land taken from his opponents.

He gave up the dictatorship around the turn of 81-80 BC (the Wikipedia articles differ on whether at the end of 81 or the start of 80), served as consul in 80 BC with Metellus Pius, and then retired to private life, dying in 78 BC. Many of his laws on the courts, the Senate and governors lasted long after him, but his march on Rome and dictatorship set an example that Pompey and Julius Caesar followed.

Q1051202.title: Second Catilinarian conspiracy
Q1051202.place: Rome; Catiline's army in Etruria (Faesulae); final battle near Pistoria (Pistoia)
paras: The Catilinarian conspiracy was an attempted coup in 63 BC by Lucius Sergius Catilina (Catiline), a patrician who had been rejected by the voters for the consulship three times. After losing the elections for 62 BC he planned to seize the consulship by force from the consuls of 63, Marcus Tullius Cicero and Gaius Antonius Hybrida. Around him gathered senators thrown out of the Senate or blocked in their careers, debtors, and men ruined by Sulla's civil war, including Sullan veterans who had fallen into debt. A former centurion, Gaius Manlius, raised an army in Etruria near Faesulae.

Cicero learned of the plot through Fulvia, the mistress of one of the conspirators. In October Crassus handed him letters warning of planned killings, and the Senate passed its emergency decree; Manlius took up arms on 27 October. An attempt on Cicero's life failed, and on 7 November, according to Wikipedia, he denounced Catiline in the Senate in the first of his Catilinarian speeches. Catiline left Rome, joined Manlius and took the insignia of a consul, and the Senate declared both men public enemies and sent Antonius against them.

In the city the praetor Publius Lentulus Sura tried to win over envoys of the Allobroges, a Gallic people. They told Cicero, who used them to obtain written proof and had them stopped at the Mulvian Bridge. Five conspirators, Lentulus, Cethegus, Statilius, Gabinius and Caeparius, were arrested and confessed. In the Senate's debate of 5 December, Julius Caesar argued against death without trial, but Cato's speech won the house over. The five were strangled in the Tullianum prison, on the Senate's advice and without trial.

Support for Catiline then fell away. In early January 62 BC his remaining force, at least 3,000 men according to Wikipedia, was caught near Pistoria by the army of Antonius, commanded by his lieutenant Marcus Petreius because Antonius was ill, and Catiline died fighting. Cicero was hailed as 'father of the fatherland', but the executions without trial were later used against him, and in 58 BC Clodius's law drove him into exile. Wikipedia notes that both main sources, Cicero's speeches and Sallust's history, are hostile to Catiline, and that modern scholars think the danger was exaggerated, though the plot was real.

Q16957926.title: Chola invasion of Srivijaya
Q16957926.place: Srivijaya: Palembang (Sumatra), Kadaram (Kedah, Malay Peninsula) and other ports of the Malacca Strait
paras: In 1025 the Chola emperor Rajendra I of southern India sent a naval expedition against Srivijaya, the trading empire of Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula that controlled the Malacca and Sunda Straits. Relations had been friendly under his father Rajaraja I, when a Srivijayan king built a Buddhist monastery at the Chola port of Nagapattinam. Why Rajendra attacked is unclear. The historian Nilakanta Sastri suggested that Srivijaya was obstructing Chola trade with China, or that Rajendra wanted to carry his conquests overseas; another theory links the war to an appeal from the Khmer king against Tambralinga, which had turned to Srivijaya for help.

Rajendra's own inscription in the great temple at Thanjavur (Tanjore) says that he despatched many ships across the sea and caught Sangrama-vijayottungavarman, the king of Kadaram, with his war elephants, and took his accumulated treasure and the jewelled Vidyadhara-torana, the arch at the war-gate of the enemy's city. It then lists the places taken, among them Pannai, Malaiyur, Ilangasogam, Talaittakkolam, Ilamuri-desam and Kadaram itself. Wikipedia reconstructs the campaign as a fast series of raids: the fleet sailed down the west coast of Sumatra and came in through the Sunda Strait, surprising a Srivijayan navy based at Kedah, then sacked the capital Palembang and its palace before striking other ports.

The Cholas did not hold most of what they plundered, but Srivijaya never recovered its old power. With its king captured, the Sailendra dynasty came to an end, and Wikipedia says no Srivijayan envoys reached China between 1028 and 1077. A Srivijayan princess who escaped became queen of Airlangga of Java, and the war opened the way for Javanese kingdoms such as Kahuripan and Kediri. Chola influence lasted for decades around Kedah, where Tamil merchant guilds also expanded.

cp02-11.title: Arab conquest of Egypt completed
cp02-11.place: Egypt: Pelusium, the Babylon fortress (Old Cairo), Heliopolis and Alexandria
paras: Between 639 and 642 an army of the Rashidun Caliphate under Amr ibn al-As took Egypt from the Byzantine Empire, ending about seven centuries of Roman rule. Egypt had only recently been recovered from a Sasanian Persian occupation, and its government was divided: Cyrus, the Chalcedonian patriarch of Alexandria, was in effect its governor, while Theodore commanded the army. Amr entered Egypt in December 639 with about 4,000 men and took Pelusium after a siege of about a month.

Reinforced to some 12,000 men, the Arabs reached Heliopolis in July 640 and defeated the Byzantines there, and besieged the great fortress of Babylon, near modern Cairo, which fell in April 641. Cyrus then negotiated the surrender of the whole country. The chronicle of John, bishop of Nikiu in Egypt, records the terms: a fixed tribute, an armistice of eleven months, the Roman troops in Alexandria to leave by sea with their property and never return, 150 soldiers and 50 civilians given as hostages, churches left alone, and the Jews allowed to stay in Alexandria. When Arab troops came to collect the tribute before the city had been told, the Alexandrians tried to stone Cyrus, who wept and said he had made the treaty to save them and their children.

Wikipedia dates the armistice's end to 28 September 642. John of Nikiu says that Theodore and the last troops then sailed for Cyprus, and that Amr entered Alexandria without a fight and was received with respect by its people, who were in great hardship. He also complains that the new rulers trebled the taxes and kept hated Byzantine officials in office. The loss of the prosperous province badly weakened the Byzantine Empire.

cp01-20.title: Octavian receives the name Augustus
paras: Octavian, the great-nephew and heir of Julius Caesar, had become the master of the Roman world after his commander Marcus Agrippa defeated Mark Antony at Actium in 31 BC and Antony and Cleopatra killed themselves during Octavian's invasion of Egypt. Years of civil war had left Rome close to lawlessness, but Roman tradition was hostile to one-man rule, and Octavian could not give up his power without risking a new war. He looked for a form of rule that kept real control in his hands while avoiding the look of a monarchy or a dictatorship.

In January 27 BC, on 13 January according to Wikipedia, he announced to the Senate that he was handing the state, its armies and its provinces back to the Senate and the Roman people. The historian Cassius Dio, writing two centuries later, says a few senators knew his real intention and applauded, while the house as a whole shouted for him to keep control. The Senate asked him to take back charge of provinces, and he accepted them for ten years, saying he would pacify them. They were the provinces that were insecure or had enemies on their borders, among them the Gallic provinces, most of Spain, Syria, Cilicia, Cyprus and Egypt, and they held most of the legions; the peaceful ones, such as Africa, Asia and Greece, went to the Senate.

On 16 January 27 BC the Senate gave him the name Augustus, 'the revered', a word used of sacred things. Dio says Octavian had wanted to be called Romulus, after the founder of Rome, but dropped the idea when it made people suspect he wanted to be king. In his own record of his deeds, the Res Gestae, Augustus wrote that in return for transferring the republic to the Senate and people he was named Augustus by a decree of the Senate, the doorposts of his house were wreathed with laurel by public decree, a civic crown was fixed above his door, and a golden shield set up in the Senate house praised his valour, clemency, justice and piety. Dio explains the laurels and the oak crown as signs that he always defeated his enemies and saved the lives of citizens.

Augustus wrote that from then on he stood above everyone in rank but had no more power than his colleagues in each office. Dio judged instead that from this time Rome was really a monarchy, because Augustus controlled both the money and the soldiers, and his ten-year command was renewed again and again until he ruled for life. Wikipedia counts him as the first Roman emperor from 27 BC; augustus became the main title of later emperors. By the summer of 27 BC he had left Rome for Gaul, and from 26 to 24 BC he governed from Tarraco in Spain while his armies fought in the north of the peninsula.

cp02-13.title: Uthman becomes caliph
paras: In 644 the second caliph, Umar, was fatally wounded by an assassin, Abu Lulu; Ameer Ali describes him as a foreigner with a grudge against the caliph, said by some to be a Zoroastrian and by others a Christian craftsman from Kufa. Rather than name a successor himself, the dying Umar handed the choice to six senior companions of the Prophet, all early emigrants from Mecca, who were to pick one of their own number: Uthman ibn Affan, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Zubayr ibn al-Awwam and Talha ibn Ubayd Allah.

William Muir's account says Umar gave the electors three days and ordered that a minority still holding out should be put to death; Wikipedia quotes a similar order from the history of al-Ya'qubi. After Umar's burial the electors met in a room beside Aisha's house, with Abu Talha guarding the door. Two days went by in argument. Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf then offered to give up his own claim if the others would accept his choice, and they all agreed, Ali last. Abd al-Rahman spent the following nights sounding out the leading men of Medina, the provincial officers who were in the city for the pilgrimage, and each elector in private. The contest narrowed to two men: Ali, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, of the clan of Hashim, and Uthman, of the clan of Umayya.

According to al-Ya'qubi, as given by Wikipedia, Abd al-Rahman asked Ali whether, as caliph, he would follow the Quran, the example of the Prophet and the practice of the two previous caliphs, Abu Bakr and Umar. Ali promised only the Quran and the Prophet's example. Uthman accepted all the conditions and was chosen. Ameer Ali writes that Ali pledged his loyalty to Uthman as soon as he was elected. Uthman was then close to seventy. A successful merchant who had been brought to Islam by Abu Bakr, he had married two of Muhammad's daughters in turn, Ruqayya and then Umm Kulthum.

Uthman reigned until 656. He handed much military authority to kinsmen such as Abd Allah ibn Amir, Mu'awiya and Abd Allah ibn Sa'd, and the conquests went on in North Africa, Iran and as far as Sindh, while Mu'awiya's new navy defeated the Byzantines at the Battle of the Masts in 655. Discontent grew in the provinces, and in 656 rebels besieged Uthman in his house in Medina and killed him.

cp02-23.title: Abbasid Caliphate founded
cp02-23.place: Kufa and the Great Zab, Iraq
paras: The Abbasids descended from Abbas, an uncle of the Prophet Muhammad, and belonged to his clan of Hashim. That link made them attractive to Muslims who resented the Umayyad caliphs, who did not come from the Prophet's family. From 718 Muhammad ibn Ali, a great-grandson of Abbas, sent agents into Persia to campaign for the return of power to the Prophet's house; the Abbasids also courted the mawali, non-Arab converts who were treated as second-class Muslims under the Umayyads. Their base was Khurasan in north-eastern Iran, far from the Umayyad heartland in Syria and full of Arab settlers and local converts who resented Umayyad rule. The family's agent there was Abu Muslim, a man of slave origin whom Muir describes as having been bought for the cause as a youth.

The revolt broke out in Khurasan in Ramadan 129 AH (June 747), when Abu Muslim raised the Abbasids' black banner at Merv; Wikipedia gives the date as 9 June and puts his force at close to 10,000 men. He drove the Umayyad governor, Nasr ibn Sayyar, out of Merv, and his general Qahtaba ibn Shabib chased the Umayyad forces west, beating them at Gorgan and Nahavand in 748. The caliph Marwan II intercepted a letter from the head of the Abbasid family, Ibrahim, to Abu Muslim and had Ibrahim arrested at Humayma, the family's village; he died in prison at Harran, whether by murder or naturally is not known. His brothers Abu al-Abbas and Abu Ja'far fled to Kufa in Iraq and hid there.

The rebels took Kufa in 749, though Qahtaba died on the way. According to Muir, Abu Salama, a leader of the movement, governed the city as 'vizier of the house of Muhammad' and kept the Abbasid brothers hidden for weeks, and some suspected that he favoured the descendants of Ali instead. To forestall a candidate from Ali's line, the Abbasid party brought Abu al-Abbas out and proclaimed him caliph in Kufa. In the Great Mosque he praised the claims of the Prophet's family, condemned the Umayyads and promised the Kufans higher pay. He became known as al-Saffah, which Muir renders 'the shedder of blood'; Muir thinks the name may have been put into the account of the speech afterwards.

Early in 750 an Abbasid army under Abu al-Abbas's uncle Abdallah ibn Ali defeated Marwan near the Great Zab river, ending Umayyad power. Marwan fled to Egypt and was killed there, and the Abbasids hunted down his family; Muir tells of about ninety Umayyads who were offered an amnesty, invited to a feast in Palestine and killed there. One prince, Abd al-Rahman, escaped and in 756 founded an independent Umayyad state in al-Andalus, which never accepted Abbasid rule. The centre of the caliphate moved from Syria to Iraq, nearer the Persian supporters on whom the new dynasty relied; Kufa served as the first capital, and in 762 the second Abbasid caliph, al-Mansur, founded Baghdad on the Tigris, a round city with the palace and great mosque at its centre. Abbasid caliphs ruled from Iraq, mostly from Baghdad, until the Mongols sacked it in 1258.

cp18-047.title: Khmer Empire founded
paras: The Khmer Empire grew out of Chenla, a set of Khmer kingdoms in what is now Cambodia. Its founder, Jayavarman II, left no inscriptions of his own; what is known of him comes from later inscriptions, above all the Sdok Kak Thom inscription of about 1052, which tells the history of a family of royal priests who served the kings' cult from 802 to 1052. Later inscriptions say he 'came from Java'. Lawrence Palmer Briggs, writing in 1951, followed the older view that he had spent time at the court of a Javanese overlord; Wikipedia notes that some historians took 'Java' to mean the Chams of Champa, and that Arlo Griffiths argued in 2013 that such inscriptions almost always mean the island of Java.

Jayavarman first ruled at Indrapura, which Wikipedia, citing the Sdok Kak Thom inscription, says he made his capital around 781 and places at Banteay Prey Nokor near Kampong Cham, in the east. He made a priest, Sivakaivalya, his chaplain and extended his power by defeating rival rulers; according to Briggs, a general named Prithivinarendra subdued the region of Malyang south-west of the Great Lake and made its people pay a perpetual tribute. He then moved his court several times, among other places to Hariharalaya near modern Roluos and to Amarendrapura, before settling on Mahendraparvata, the mountain now called Phnom Kulen, north-east of the later Angkor.

In 802, on Mahendraparvata, Jayavarman held the ceremony that historians treat as the start of the Angkor period. The Sdok Kak Thom inscription, as translated by Briggs, says he invited a Brahman skilled in magic, Hiranyadama, to perform a rite so that the Khmer country would no longer owe allegiance to Java and would have a single sovereign, a chakravartin or 'universal ruler'. Jayavarman also took the title devaraja, 'god-king', and a royal linga, the emblem of Shiva and of royal power, was installed as the centre of a state cult; Briggs identifies the pyramid temple of Rong Chen on the Kulen plateau as its first home. Hiranyadama taught the ritual to Sivakaivalya, whose family kept the cult for two and a half centuries.

Jayavarman later moved back to Hariharalaya and died there. Wikipedia gives his death as 835; Briggs cites an inscription from Tuol Ta Pec that places it in 850. His successors kept enlarging the kingdom, and Yasovarman I (reigned 889 to 915) founded Yasodharapura, the first city on the site of Angkor. For more than six hundred years the Khmer capital stayed in this region; the empire is usually said to have lasted until the fall of Angkor to the Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya in 1431.

cp18-089.title: Samanid dynasty begins to rule Transoxiana
paras: The Samanid family took its name from Saman-khuda, the lord of the village of Saman in the province of Balkh, in what is now northern Afghanistan; the family claimed descent from Bahram Chobin, a Sasanian general of the late sixth century. Saman-khuda gave up Zoroastrianism for Islam under the Arab governor of Khurasan, Asad ibn Abdallah, and named his son Asad after him.

Asad's four sons, Nuh, Ahmad, Yahya and Ilyas, helped to put down the revolt of Rafi ibn al-Layth, which had broken out at Samarkand in 806, and then served the future caliph al-Ma'mun while he was in Khurasan. In 819, at the caliph's wish, the governor of Khurasan, Ghassan ibn Abbad, rewarded them with governorships: Nuh received Samarkand, Ahmad the Ferghana valley, Yahya Shash (the Tashkent region) and Ilyas Herat. The brothers ruled as Abbasid governors under the authority of the governor of Khurasan, a post held from 821 by the Tahirid family.

The family soon lost Herat, but in Transoxiana its rule became hereditary. Nuh took Isfijab from the steppe Turks in about 840, and after the deaths of his brothers Ahmad held most of the region; Barthold notes that Bukhara came under Samanid rule only in 874, and that in 875 Ahmad's son Nasr received a diploma from the caliph for the whole of Transoxiana. Nasr's brother Ismail, who had won a struggle with him and united the family under his rule after Nasr's death in 892, made Bukhara his capital, defeated the Saffarid ruler Amr ibn al-Layth near Balkh in 900, and was then recognised by the caliph as ruler of all Khurasan and Transoxiana; under him the Samanids became in effect independent of the Abbasids.

The Samanids ruled until 999 from Bukhara, which was said to rival Baghdad. They wrote their science and religion in Arabic but revived Persian language and literature, patronising poets and scholars such as Rudaki, Ferdowsi and Avicenna, and Wikipedia counts their state as part of the 'Iranian Intermezzo', a Persian renaissance within the Islamic world.

cp18-090.title: Karakhanids take Bukhara; the Samanid state ends
paras: By the late tenth century the Samanid amirs of Bukhara had lost most of their power to their own Turkish slave commanders, the ghulams. One of them, Alp Tigin, seized Ghazna in 962, and his successor Sabuktigin took over the Samanid provinces south of the Oxus, the core of what became the Ghaznavid state. From the north-east came the Karakhanids, Turkic rulers of the Semirechye who had recently become Muslims. In 992 the Karakhanid Harun Bughra Khan took Bukhara, but he died soon after and the Samanids returned.

In February 999, according to W. Barthold, the commanders Faiq and Begtuzun deposed and blinded the amir Mansur II and set up his younger brother Abd al-Malik II. Sabuktigin's son Mahmud then defeated them and took all of Khurasan, and Abd al-Malik and Faiq fled to Bukhara. The Karakhanid Nasr ibn Ali, known as the Ilak, now decided to finish off the dynasty. Barthold writes that the government ordered the preachers of Bukhara's mosques to call the people to arms, but the townspeople took the advice of religious scholars who said that Muslims were not obliged to get themselves killed in a fight over worldly goods. Nasr announced that he came as a friend and protector of the Samanids; Begtuzun and another commander went over to his camp and were arrested.

On 23 October 999, by Barthold's date, Nasr entered Bukhara without opposition and seized the Samanid treasury. Abd al-Malik and the other members of the family were sent as prisoners to Uzgen in the Ferghana valley, and Nasr left his own governors in Bukhara and Samarkand. Barthold remarks that the fall of the famous dynasty passed amid general indifference.

The Samanid lands were divided: Mahmud's Ghaznavids kept Khurasan and the Karakhanids took Transoxiana, with the Oxus as the border between them. One prince, Ismail al-Muntasir, escaped from prison, according to Barthold in women's clothes, and fought for several years to restore the state, briefly retaking Bukhara and Samarkand, until an Arab chief near Merv killed him in 1005. Barthold saw the event as the end of rule by the native Iranian population in Central Asia; from then on Turkic dynasties ruled Transoxiana.

cp18-051.title: Anawrahta becomes king of Pagan
paras: In the early eleventh century Pagan was a small kingdom in the dry zone of Upper Burma. Anawrahta's father, Kunhsaw Kyaunghpyu, had taken its throne from King Nyaung-u Sawrahan, but he was overthrown in turn by Nyaung-u Sawrahan's two sons, Kyiso and Sokkate, who forced him to become a monk. The young prince, called Min Saw, lived near the monastery with his parents and kept his rank at court. Kyiso died, according to G. E. Harvey's history in a hunting accident, and Sokkate became king.

In 1044 Min Saw raised a following at Mount Popa, challenged Sokkate to single combat and killed him at Myinkaba near Pagan. Wikipedia says he first offered the throne to his father, who had long been a monk and refused it, and then took it himself under the name Anawrahta, a Burmese form of the Sanskrit Aniruddha. Harvey wrote that with his reign Burmese history begins to be less a matter of guesswork; his is the first reign whose events can be checked against stone inscriptions. The Burmese chronicles do not agree on his dates: Arthur Phayre's History of Burma of 1883, following an older chronicle reckoning, placed the whole reign earlier, ending it around the middle of the eleventh century, while Harvey and modern historians give 1044.

As king, Anawrahta built weirs and canals around Kyaukse that turned the dry country near Pagan into the rice granary of Upper Burma. He was converted to Theravada Buddhism by Shin Arahan, a monk from the Mon city of Thaton, and drove out the priests of the older Ari sect. In 1057 his armies took Thaton after a three-month siege; the chronicles say the cause was its king Manuha's refusal to give him the Buddhist scriptures, while Wikipedia reports historians who see it as a demand for submission. Manuha and his family were carried off to Pagan with artisans, relics and scriptures, though the historian Michael Aung-Thwin has argued that Thaton's influence on Pagan is largely a later legend. Anawrahta also took tribute from the Shan hills and northern Arakan and marched to the Dali kingdom in Yunnan.

Anawrahta died in 1077. He was the first ruler to unite the whole Irrawaddy valley, and the dynasty he founded ruled Pagan until 1287. The Shwezigon pagoda, which he began and which his son Kyanzittha finished, still draws worshippers to its relics, and he is regarded as the father of the Burmese nation and the king who established Theravada Buddhism in Burma.

cp02-16.title: Umayyad Caliphate founded
paras: When the caliph Uthman was murdered in 656, Ali was recognised as caliph in Medina, but Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the long-serving governor of Syria and a kinsman of Uthman from the Umayyad clan, refused to accept him and demanded revenge for Uthman's death. Their armies fought to a stalemate at Siffin in 657, and Ali's agreement to settle the dispute by arbitration split his own camp: the Kharijites broke away from him, Iraqi nobles began to go over to Mu'awiya, and Mu'awiya's ally Amr ibn al-As took Egypt in 658. In July 660 Mu'awiya's Syrian allies recognised him as caliph in Jerusalem.

In January 661 a Kharijite, Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, struck Ali down at the mosque in Kufa, and Ali's eldest son Hasan was proclaimed caliph there. Mu'awiya marched on Kufa with a large army. William Muir's account says the Kufans raised 40,000 men and Hasan sent ahead a vanguard of 12,000 under Qays ibn Sa'd, but when a rumour spread at al-Mada'in that Qays had been killed, Hasan's troops mutinied and plundered his tent; Wikipedia adds that many of his commanders and tribal chiefs had been won over by Mu'awiya's promises of money and pardon, and that Hasan was wounded in an attempt on his life.

Hasan then made peace and handed the caliphate to Mu'awiya. According to Wikipedia, the treaty promised a general amnesty and said that a council would choose the caliph after Mu'awiya's death, while Syed Ameer Ali wrote that it gave the succession to Hasan's brother Husayn; Muir says Hasan also kept the Kufan treasury and retired to Medina. Mu'awiya entered Kufa and received the allegiance of the Iraqis, an event Muslim tradition called the 'year of unification' of the community and usually counted as the start of his reign. He went back to Syria as sole caliph, and Damascus became the capital of the empire, with Syria and its Arab tribes as the base of the new dynasty.

Mu'awiya ruled for about twenty years, until 680, governing Iraq through powerful governors such as al-Mughira at Kufa and Ziyad ibn Abihi, and continuing the wars against Byzantium. In 676, in a step without precedent, he had his son Yazid recognised as his successor, which made the caliphate hereditary in his family. The Umayyads ruled from Damascus until the Abbasid revolution of 750; opposition to their rule, above all from Ali's supporters, fed later civil wars, and Shia tradition remembers Mu'awiya for fighting Ali at Siffin and for naming Yazid, whose forces killed Ali's son Husayn at Karbala.

Q110970851.title: Siege of Bukhara (1220)
paras: In 1218 the governor of Otrar, with the consent of the Khwarazm-shah Muhammad II, seized a Mongol trade caravan, and when Genghis Khan sent envoys to the shah one of them was executed. In 1219 Genghis left the war against the Jin in China and invaded the Khwarazmian Empire. The shah chose not to risk open battle and spread his troops among the garrisons of his main cities. At Otrar Genghis divided his army: one force stayed to besiege the town, his son Jochi went down the Syr Darya, a small detachment went up the river towards Khujand, and Genghis himself, with his youngest son Tolui and the main army, struck west towards Bukhara, far from the frontier. Wikipedia gives modern estimates of 30,000 to 50,000 men for this force.

The Mongols crossed the Kyzylkum desert, which contemporaries thought impassable for a large army. On the way, according to W. Barthold, the fortress of Zarnuq surrendered on a promise of safety and had its walls pulled down, and the people of Nur, who at first took the Mongols for a trading caravan, had to leave their town while it was plundered and then pay 1,500 dinars. Barthold dates the arrival at Bukhara to February 1220, following the contemporary writers Ibn al-Athir and Juzjani; Wikipedia gives 7 February. The size of the garrison is uncertain: Barthold reports 12,000 horsemen in Juzjani, 30,000 men in Nasawi and 20,000 for the field force alone in Juvaini, while Wikipedia cites a modern estimate of only 2,000 to 5,000.

On the third day of the siege the troops of the garrison tried to break out and cut their way through the Mongol lines, but they were pursued and destroyed; Barthold says their commander, Inanch Khan, got across the Amu Darya with only a few men. Abandoned by its defenders, the town surrendered, sending a deputation led by its qadi. The Mongols entered on 10 February according to Ibn al-Athir, a date Wikipedia follows, or on 16 February according to Juzjani. About 400 horsemen held out in the citadel for another twelve days; the townspeople were made to fill in its moat, and when it fell every defender was killed.

The inhabitants were then driven out with nothing but the clothes they wore, while the Mongols plundered the town and killed anyone who stayed behind. Craftsmen were taken for the Mongols' service and men of fighting age were forced to march with the army; Barthold notes that prisoners who could not keep up on the road to Samarkand were killed. Most of Bukhara burned. Wikipedia says the Mongols set the fire to drive out the last defenders, while Barthold thought it the near-inevitable result of plundering a crowded town, with only the great mosque and some brick palaces left standing. Barthold also rejected as unbelievable the story, told by Juvaini and quoted in Wikipedia, that Genghis spoke from the pulpit calling himself the punishment of God. Bukhara recovered: within about two decades it was again a centre of trade and learning.

Q7510363.title: Siege of Samarkand
paras: Samarkand, the chief city of Transoxiana, was the centre of the Khwarazm-shah Muhammad II's defence against Genghis Khan's invasion, and he gave it a larger garrison than any other town. Its commander was Tughay Khan, a brother of the shah's mother Terken Khatun. The garrison's size is uncertain: W. Barthold lists 110,000 men with twenty elephants in Juvaini, 40,000 in Nasawi, 50,000 in Ibn al-Athir and 60,000 in Juzjani, while Wikipedia gives about 30,000 Qanqli Turks and 50,000 local troops with twenty elephants.

After taking Bukhara in February 1220, Genghis marched up the Zarafshan valley, leaving small detachments to besiege the forts he passed. He reached Samarkand in March and was joined by his sons Chagatai and Ogedei, who brought crowds of captives from the fall of Otrar. Barthold, following Juvaini, says the Mongols drew up their prisoners in battle order, with a standard for every ten men, so that the besieging army looked enormous.

On the third day the defenders made a sortie and were caught in an ambush. The contemporary writers Ibn al-Athir and Juzjani say it was made by the townspeople and destroyed to the last man, with losses of 70,000 and 50,000 respectively; Juvaini says it was made by the Turkish troops, who lost 1,000 men, the figure Wikipedia gives. Soon afterwards the Turks and the townspeople decided to give in: on the fifth day of the siege according to Juvaini, on 17 March according to Juzjani, and on 16 March in Wikipedia's account. A deputation led by the qadi and the shaykh al-Islam surrendered the town, the Mongols pulled down its fortifications, and the inhabitants were driven out while the town was sacked, except for the clergy and the people under their protection.

The citadel held out a little longer. Barthold says the Mongols took it by storm after breaking a canal known as the 'leaden watercourse', whose water probably undermined part of the walls, that the night before about 1,000 men broke out under Alp Khan and escaped, and that the last 1,000 defenders were killed in the great mosque, which was burnt; Wikipedia says the citadel held for about a month, that 1,000 men escaped across the Amu Darya and that about 3,000 were executed. The Turkish troops who had gone over to the Mongols were then surrounded and massacred with Tughay Khan. According to Barthold, 30,000 craftsmen were handed out to Genghis's sons and relatives and as many men taken for siege work, and the remaining inhabitants were allowed back after paying a ransom of 200,000 dinars. Genghis left Yelu Ahai to govern Samarkand and Bukhara; the city recovered only slowly, until Timur made it his capital in 1370.

Q3269760.title: Battle of Indus
paras: After Genghis Khan's armies had taken Bukhara, Samarkand and the other cities of the Khwarazmian Empire, the shah Muhammad II fled west and died on an island in the Caspian Sea in December 1220. His eldest son, Jalal al-Din, took up the fight. He gathered an army at Ghazni and in the autumn of 1221 beat a Mongol force under Shigi Qutuqu at Parwan. But his allies then quarrelled over the spoils, and many of his troops, mostly Afghans under Sayf al-Din Ighrak, left him. Unable to face Genghis, who was marching against him with the main Mongol army, Jalal al-Din fell back to the Indus, meaning to cross into India.

The Mongols caught him on the west bank before he could get across; Barthold notes that only one boat had arrived, and it was broken by the waves. Nasawi, Jalal al-Din's biographer, dates the battle to Wednesday 24 November 1221, the date Wikipedia gives; other sources give the month of Rajab, which Barthold, following Raverty, thought improbable. Jalal al-Din held the centre himself, with his uncle Amin Malik on the right wing; Wikipedia says his army numbered about 30,000 and Genghis's at least 50,000. Jalal al-Din's centre at first threw the Mongols into confusion; Nasawi even claims Genghis took to flight. But a reserve of 10,000 picked Mongol warriors fell on the right wing, and Wikipedia adds that an elite force climbed a ridge to take the Khwarazmian left in the flank; the line broke and Amin Malik was killed as he fled.

Seeing the battle lost, Jalal al-Din rode his horse into the river and crossed to the far bank. Wikipedia repeats the story that Genghis forbade his archers to shoot and praised the courage of his enemy. About 4,000 of his soldiers reached the far bank with him, and Barthold says 300 horsemen carried far downstream joined him three days later; many others were killed in the water. His son of seven or eight was captured and killed, and Barthold says that Jalal al-Din had his mother, his wife and the other women of his family thrown into the river so that they would not fall into Mongol hands.

Genghis did not cross the Indus at once. A Mongol force of 20,000 sent after Jalal al-Din the next year got as far as Multan and turned back in the summer heat, and the Mongols spent 1222 taking the mountain fortresses of the region. Jalal al-Din stayed in India for about three years, then returned west to rebuild Khwarazmian rule in Iran; the battle ended Genghis's campaign against the Khwarazmian Empire, and Genghis was back in Mongolia in 1224 or 1225.

cp18-049.title: Lý dynasty founded
paras: In 1009 Lê Long Đĩnh, the unpopular last ruler of the Early Lê dynasty of Đại Cồ Việt, died, leaving a crown prince too young to rule. Members of the court, among them the official Đào Cam Mộc and the Buddhist monk Vạn Hạnh, decided instead to put the general Lý Công Uẩn on the throne. Born in 974 in the Cổ Pháp area, Lý Công Uẩn had been adopted at the age of three by Lý Khánh Văn, a monk of the Cổ Pháp pagoda, whose surname he took; the Zen master Vạn Hạnh had noticed him as a gifted child. He joined the palace guard and rose to command it. His accession founded the Lý dynasty; he reigned as Lý Thái Tổ.

The capital was then at Hoa Lư, in hilly country, where the Đinh dynasty's founder had placed it for safety and the Lê had kept it. In 1010 the new king issued an edict announcing that he would move the capital to Đại La, the site of the citadel built under Chinese rule. Citing Chinese dynasties that had moved their capitals for the good of the state, he blamed the Đinh and Lê for clinging to Hoa Lư, saying their dynasties had been short-lived and the people ruined. Đại La, he wrote, lay at the heart of the country, shaped like 'a coiled-up dragon, a squatting tiger', on broad, level and well-raised ground safe from floods, a fit capital for ten thousand generations. He renamed it Thăng Long, 'Soaring Dragon'.

The Lý dynasty ruled until 1225, from 1054 under the state name Đại Việt. Its move of the capital had a lasting effect: Thăng Long, the later Hanoi, remained the capital under the Trần, Lê and Mạc dynasties, and after the Nguyễn moved the court to Huế it became the capital again in 1945. Wikipedia's article dates the edict to 1009 in a caption but to 1010 in its text; the Vietnamese government's Hanoi portal gives 1010.

Q14750447.title: Mongol conquest of Western Xia
paras: Western Xia, or Xi Xia, was a state ruled by the Tangut people in what is now north-western China, founded in 1038 and covering roughly today's Ningxia, Gansu and neighbouring regions; since the early twelfth century it had been a vassal of the Jin dynasty. As Temujin, the future Genghis Khan, united the Mongol tribes, Western Xia gave refuge to defeated rivals of his, among them the Kerait leader Nilqa Senggum. In 1205, using this as a pretext, the Mongols raided Western Xia for the first time, plundering border settlements and returning with much booty; H. H. Howorth's history of the Mongols says they razed a strong fort and sacked a town. A second raid followed in 1207.

In 1209 Genghis invaded in earnest. The Jin emperor refused to help his vassal. The Mongols defeated the Xia field army, Howorth says capturing one of its generals, forced the pass through the Helan Mountains and in May laid siege to the capital, Yinchuan. The city held out for months, and the attackers' attempt to use the Yellow River against it went wrong: according to Wikipedia the Mongols diverted the river to flood the city, but the dike broke and their own camp was flooded; Howorth says the defenders opened the dikes. Even so, with its crops ruined and no help coming from the Jin, the Xia ruler, Emperor Xiangzong, submitted in January 1210, accepting Mongol supremacy and giving Genghis one of his daughters in marriage, along with tribute.

For the next decade Western Xia was a Mongol vassal and fought alongside the Mongols against the Jin. But when Genghis asked for troops for his war on the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219, the Xia court refused, and it later sought alliances with the Jin and Song. Genghis returned in 1225 to punish it, destroying its cities one after another, defeating a large Xia army near the frozen Yellow River and besieging Yinchuan in 1227. He died in August 1227 while the siege was still going on, and his death was kept secret. In September the last Xia emperor surrendered and was executed, and the Mongols sacked the capital and massacred its people. Older accounts summarised by Howorth differ on the ruler's fate, one saying he was carried off in chains and another that his own people killed him, but agree that the Tangut state was destroyed.

cp03-09.title: Death of Genghis Khan
cp03-09.place: Liupan mountains, during the siege of the Western Xia capital
paras: In 1225 Genghis Khan, back from his war against the Khwarazmian Empire, went to punish the Tangut state of Western Xia, his former vassal, for refusing him troops and turning to his enemies. His armies destroyed its cities one by one and in 1227 besieged its capital, Yinchuan. While the siege went on, Genghis campaigned in the Liupan mountains to the south and prepared to attack the Jin. The besieged emperor agreed to surrender but asked for a month to prepare gifts.

It was there, in August 1227, that Genghis died. H. H. Howorth's history says he fell ill in his summer camp in the Liupan mountains, with only his youngest son Tolui beside him, and that the Chinese and Persian historians seem agreed that he died a natural death. Other stories circulated: Marco Polo wrote that he died of an infected arrow wound, the Galician-Volhynian Chronicle that the Tanguts killed him in battle, the friar Carpini that he was struck by lightning, and later Mongol chronicles linked his death to a captured Tangut princess, one even saying she stabbed him. Wikipedia concludes that the cause remains uncertain.

Howorth reports that before he died Genghis divided his lands among his sons and named Ogedei to rule over them all, and urged that the Tanguts be wiped out. His death was kept secret so as not to endanger the campaign. In September the last Xia emperor surrendered and was killed, and the Mongols sacked Yinchuan and massacred its people. Genghis's body was carried back to Mongolia; according to Rashid al-Din, as reported by Howorth, the escort killed everyone it met on the way so that the news would not spread, and he was buried at Burkhan Khaldun. Tolui acted as regent until Ogedei was chosen Great Khan in 1229.

cp03-10.title: Ögedei becomes Great Khan
paras: Ogedei was the third son of Genghis Khan. During the war against the Khwarazmian Empire his elder brothers Jochi and Chagatai quarrelled so badly over the siege of Gurganj that Genghis gave Ogedei the command, and after further quarrels between the two elder sons Ogedei was chosen as heir, a choice his father confirmed. When Genghis died in 1227 (Jochi had died a year or two earlier), the princes returned to their own lands, and for two years the youngest son, Tolui, who by Mongol custom held his father's home territory, governed as regent.

In 1229 a kurultai, an assembly of the Mongol princes and chiefs, met at Khodoe Aral on the Kherlen River to choose the new Great Khan. According to H. H. Howorth's history, many favoured Tolui, and Chagatai as the eldest surviving son had a claim under Mongol rules of inheritance, but Genghis's wish was decisive. Ogedei held back, for forty days in Howorth's account, while Wikipedia says he declined three times as the ritual required; he was proclaimed on 13 September 1229, the date Wikipedia gives. Howorth describes Chagatai and their uncle leading him to the throne, Tolui handing him the cup, and the assembly bowing nine times and hailing him as Kaan, while the princes swore never to put a ruler from any other branch of the family on the throne. Chagatai continued to support him.

Ogedei distributed his father's treasure among the nobles and, according to Howorth, sent forty young women to serve Genghis in the next world. With the help of his father's Khitan adviser Yelu Chucai, who told him that an empire conquered on horseback could not be governed on horseback, he set fixed taxes and began to organise a civil administration. He then turned the Mongols' strength back on the Jin: by 1232 the Jin emperor was besieged in Kaifeng, and the Jin dynasty was destroyed in 1234. Ogedei ruled until his death in December 1241, a reign in which the Mongol armies also invaded Korea, renewed the war in Iran, subdued the western steppes and penetrated deep into Europe.

cp03-11.title: Jin dynasty falls: siege of Caizhou
paras: The siege of Caizhou was the last major battle of the Mongol war against the Jin, the Jurchen-led dynasty that ruled northern China. The war had begun with Genghis Khan's invasion in 1211; the Mongols took the Jin capital Zhongdu (Beijing) in 1215, and the Jin moved their capital south to Bianjing (Kaifeng). Genghis's successor Ogedei renewed the war in 1230, and when the Mongols besieged Kaifeng the Jin emperor, Aizong, left the city. He reached Guide on 26 February 1233 and moved on to Caizhou, in southern Henan, on 3 August. According to H. H. Howorth's history, Kaifeng was then handed over to the Mongol general Subutai by a rebel commander, who also sent him the empresses and some 500 members of the imperial family.

Howorth says Aizong arrived at Caizhou with an escort of only 300 men, made his kinsman Wanyan Hushahu commander, and gathered about 10,000 horsemen, while crowds of refugees filled the town. He asked the Southern Song for supplies, warning them that they would be the Mongols' next target, but the Song rebuffed him and joined the Mongols instead. The Mongols arrived before Caizhou in December 1233. Howorth names their commander as Tachar and says the Song sent 20,000 troops under Meng Gong and 300,000 sacks of rice. Meng Gong drained a lake beside the town and stormed a fortified tower in it, and the allies then took the outer wall. Inside, the defenders boiled leather for food and, Howorth writes, were reduced to cannibalism.

Seeing no way to escape, Aizong abdicated on 9 February 1234, the date Wikipedia gives, in favour of Wanyan Chenglin, a general of the imperial clan, telling him (in Howorth's account) that he himself was too stout to ride. Mongol and Song troops broke into the city that same day, while the new emperor was still being installed. Aizong killed himself; Howorth says he hanged himself in a house he had ordered to be set on fire, and that Hushahu drowned himself with about 500 soldiers rather than surrender. Chenglin, whose reign lasted less than a day, died in the fighting according to Wikipedia, while Howorth says his own soldiers killed him soon afterwards. Howorth also dates the fall to May 1234, not February.

The fall of Caizhou ended the Jin dynasty, and Howorth records that the Mongols and the Song divided Aizong's remains. The alliance did not last: a Song commander murdered a Mongol envoy, and Song armies moved into Henan and took back the old capitals of Kaifeng, Luoyang and Chang'an, but the Mongols drove them out. In 1234 Ogedei announced the conquest of the Southern Song as one of his next aims.

Q1981024.title: Siege of Ryazan
paras: In the autumn of 1237 a Mongol army under Batu Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, invaded the Rus' principality of Ryazan, the first Rus' state it attacked. According to the Novgorod Chronicle, the invaders first camped on a river at the edge of the principality and sent a sorceress and two men to demand a tenth of everything: of people, princes and horses. The princes of Ryazan, with those of Murom and Pronsk, rode out to meet them at the Voronezh and answered that the Mongols could have everything only when none of them was left alive. Prince Yuri Igorevich of Ryazan asked the Grand Prince of Vladimir, Yuri Vsevolodovich, for help, but none came; the chronicle says Yuri of Vladimir preferred to fight on his own.

The Mongols defeated the Ryazan vanguard on the Voronezh River and on 16 December 1237 laid siege to the capital, the town now called Old Ryazan, some 50 km from the modern city. They surrounded it with a stockade; H. H. Howorth's history adds that they mounted siege engines on it. The townspeople beat off the first attacks, but the catapults broke down the defences, and on 21 December the Mongols stormed the walls. They killed Prince Yuri and his wife and nearly all the people, men, women, children, monks and priests alike, and burned the town; the bishop escaped, having left, the chronicle says, at the moment the town was surrounded. Excavations in 1915 and 1979 found 97 severed heads at the site of a church and 143 bodies in mass graves. Another prince of Ryazan, Roman, who had kept his men in the field, was killed with a commander sent from Vladimir in a battle at Kolomna.

Old Ryazan never recovered its place: in the 14th century, worn down by repeated Tatar raids, the princes moved their capital to Pereyaslavl-Ryazansky, which was renamed Ryazan in 1778. From Ryazan Batu's army marched into the principality of Vladimir-Suzdal. It took Moscow, then still a small town, stormed and burned Vladimir, where the Grand Prince's family died in the burning cathedral, and caught Yuri Vsevolodovich himself on the River Sit, where he was killed.

cp18-054.title: Sukhothai Kingdom founded
paras: In the early 13th century Sukhothai, in the north of the central plain of present-day Thailand, was a town under the Khmer Empire of Angkor; Wikipedia describes it as a trading centre of Lavo, itself under Khmer overlordship, and W. A. R. Wood's History of Siam (preface dated 1924) as the northern capital of the Khmer empire. A Khmer-style town had stood there since about 1200. Tai-speaking peoples had been settling in the region for centuries and had already formed small states further north.

In 1238, according to tradition, Tai led by Pho Khun Bang Klang Hao, a local chief, rose against the Khmer governor with the help of an ally, Pho Khun Pha Mueang. Wood says the Khmer king sent a general, Khlon Lamphong, to restore order, but the two chiefs defeated him in a pitched battle and entered Sukhothai. Bang Klang Hao was consecrated king under the name Si Inthrathit, a title the Khmer king had originally given to Pha Mueang, and became the first ruler of the Phra Ruang dynasty.

Si Inthrathit spent his reign extending his lands at the expense of the Khmer and his western neighbours. Wood suggests he was helped by a wave of Tai refugees from Yunnan after Kublai Khan conquered the kingdom of Nanzhao in 1254. One of his sons, Ram Khamhaeng, won fame by defeating the ruler of Chot in single combat on elephants. Wikipedia says that by Si Inthrathit's death in 1270 Sukhothai held the whole upper valley of the Chao Phraya; Wood says the year of his death is not known. He was followed by his son Ban Mueang and then by Ram Khamhaeng, under whom the kingdom reached its greatest extent.

Thai tradition calls Sukhothai the first Thai kingdom, although historians now agree that Tai history began earlier. In 1349 it was invaded by the neighbouring Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya, and after decades as its tributary it was annexed in 1438. The ruins of its capital are now the Sukhothai Historical Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Q815162.title: Siege of Kyiv (1240)
paras: After destroying Ryazan and Vladimir in 1237 and 1238, the Mongol army of Batu Khan turned south-west. In 1239 it took Pereyaslav and Chernigov, and Batu's cousin Mongke, who later became Great Khan, came before Kyiv and demanded its surrender. Kyiv, with its white walls and gilded church domes, had long been the chief city of the Rus' and the seat of their metropolitan, though it had been badly damaged in earlier wars between the princes. The Mongol envoys were killed. Grand Prince Michael of Chernigov then fled to Hungary, Rostislav of Smolensk seized the city and was in turn driven out by Daniel of Galicia-Volhynia. When the Mongols returned in November 1240, under the tactical command of the general Subutai, Daniel was in Hungary seeking allies and the defence was led by his commander, Dmytro.

Batu destroyed a force of Black Hood auxiliaries coming to relieve the city, and his whole army camped before its gates. According to the dates compared by the historian Alexander Maiorov, the siege lasted nine days. On 28 November the Mongols set up catapults near a gate where woods came almost up to the walls and bombarded the city for several days; H. H. Howorth's history says the din of the Mongols' carts, camels and horses drowned the voices of the people inside. On 6 December the walls were breached and fighting went on in the streets until nightfall. Dmytro was wounded by an arrow, and the defenders fell back to the centre of the city, where crowds took refuge in the Church of the Tithes. When the Mongols made their final assault, part of the church collapsed under the weight of the people on it, crushing many.

The Mongols plundered the city and killed most of its people: Wikipedia gives a figure of about 2,000 survivors out of 50,000 inhabitants, and says only six of forty major buildings were left standing. Dmytro was spared for his courage. Howorth notes that the Church of the Tithes, the tomb of Olga and the Pechersk monastery were wrecked or looted. The chronicles of the Rus' disagree widely over details and dates; a Pskov account of a ten-week siege is now considered invented.

The fall of Kyiv forced Galicia and Volhynia to accept Mongol overlordship and opened the way for Batu's invasion of Poland and Hungary, which stopped only in 1242, after news came of Ogedei Khan's death. Within a few years the Golden Horde was collecting tribute in Kyiv through its own officials, and the Rus' princes had to travel to Batu's capital at Sarai to be confirmed in their lands.

cp03-18.title: Kublai is proclaimed Great Khan
paras: Kublai was a grandson of Genghis Khan and the second son of Tolui and Sorghaghtani Beki. His elder brother Mongke, Great Khan from 1251, made him viceroy of northern China, where he surrounded himself with Chinese advisers and Buddhist monks, and in 1256 he built himself a new residence north of the Great Wall at Kaiping, also known as Shangdu. In 1259 Mongke died while campaigning against the Song in Sichuan without naming a successor. He had left their youngest brother, Ariq Boke, in charge of the Mongol capital Karakorum, while Kublai was besieging Wuchang on the Yangtze and another brother, Hulagu, was fighting in the Middle East.

Kublai at first kept the news secret and continued the siege. The Song minister Jia Sidao offered him a yearly tribute of silver and silk and the Yangtze as the frontier; Kublai refused at first, but when word came that Ariq Boke was raising troops to take the throne, he accepted terms and hurried north. Ariq Boke had the support of most of Mongke's family and of the Ogedei, Chagatai and Jochi lines. In 1260 Kublai held his own kurultai at Kaiping, attended by fewer princes; H. H. Howorth's history lists among them his brother Mukeh, Ogedei's son Kadan and Togatshar, and says the descendants of Jochi and Chagatai and the absent Hulagu were not summoned. The assembly elected Kublai Great Khan; Howorth gives his age as 44. It was the first kurultai to proclaim a Great Khan outside the Mongol homeland. Ariq Boke was proclaimed Great Khan at Karakorum by his own kurultai; the Toluid Civil War article and Howorth place this after Kublai's election, the Kublai Khan article before it.

The two claimants went to war. Kublai held the farmland of northern China, cut most of the routes that fed Karakorum and courted his Chinese subjects with lower taxes and Chinese-style institutions. His armies defeated Ariq Boke's generals in the west, and Kublai beat him in 1261 at Shimultai. Abandoned by his ally Alghu of the Chagatai Khanate, Ariq Boke surrendered at Shangdu in 1264 and died in captivity in 1266. The victory did not reunite the empire: the khans of the west did not attend the kurultai Kublai called to confirm his title, Ogedei's grandson Kaidu rose against him from 1269, and the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate and the Ilkhanate became in practice independent states, while Kublai concentrated on China, where in 1271 he proclaimed the Yuan dynasty.

Q1319855.title: Battle of Kirina
paras: After the collapse of the old Ghana Empire, weakened by internal strife and by the intervention of the Almoravids in the 11th century, smaller states in the western Sahel competed to replace it. Among them were the Sosso of the Kaniaga kingdom and the Mandinka of the Upper Niger. Under their king Soumaoro (Sumanguru) Kanté the Sosso took Koumbi Saleh, the former Ghana capital, and conquered the Mandinka among others. The French colonial scholar Maurice Delafosse, writing in 1922, dated the Sosso capture of Ghana to 1203 and their annexation of the Manding to about 1224, but Wikipedia notes that later scholars have rejected much of Delafosse's reconstruction of this period.

The battle is known mainly from the Epic of Sundiata, the oral tradition handed down by Mandinka griots. In it Sundiata, a Mandinka prince who was crippled as a child, had gone into exile with his mother Sogolon to escape his half-brother, and found refuge and high office with the king of Mema. When Soumaoro conquered the Mandinka, messengers found Sundiata and persuaded him to return. He came back with an army given by the king of Mema, and on the plain of Siby he and the young war leaders of the Mandinka, among them Tiramakhan Traore, swore a pact to free their country. Sundiata built a coalition of smaller kingdoms against the Sosso.

The two armies met at Kirina, in what is now the Koulikoro Region of Mali, in about 1235, and Sundiata's forces won a complete victory. In the epic, Soumaoro is a sorcerer-king; Sundiata discovers that his protective animal is the rooster and wounds him with an arrow tipped with a cock's spur, and Soumaoro flees the field and disappears into the Koulikoro mountains. Delafosse, by contrast, wrote that Sundiata defeated and killed him not far from Koulikoro. After the battle Sundiata marched on and razed Sosso.

Kirina is often taken as the beginning of the Mali Empire, which controlled much of West Africa for the next two centuries. Sundiata took over the states the Sosso had conquered, was the first Mandinka ruler to take the title mansa, and set up his capital at Niani; his generals conquered the lands of old Ghana and, under Tiramakhan, the kingdom of Jolof and much of Senegambia. Delafosse dated the destruction of Ghana by Sundiata to 1240. Arab writers of the following century, among them Ibn Khaldun, knew Sundiata as Mari Djata; Flora Shaw's 1905 history, drawing on them, says he overthrew the Sosso, conquered Ghana and reigned for 25 years. Sundiata died in about 1255.

cp18-074.title: Solomonic dynasty restored
paras: For several generations before 1270 the Christian highlands of Ethiopia were ruled by the Zagwe kings, from an Agaw people, who had replaced the royal house of Aksum. Yekuno Amlak was a ruler from Bete Amhara, lord of Geshen and Ambassel near Lake Hayq, where he was educated at the monastery of Istifanos. Later texts written to support his dynasty said that he descended in the male line from the kings of Aksum, and through them from Menelik I, the son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, and they portrayed the Zagwe as usurpers who were not of the line of Israel.

Traditional history says Yekuno Amlak escaped from imprisonment by the Zagwe king on Mount Malot, gathered support in Amhara and Shewa, and, with considerable help from the Muslim Sultanate of Shewa, defeated the Zagwe king at the Battle of Ansata. Wikipedia dates his seizure of power to 1270; Budge gives 1268 or 1270. Which king he overthrew is disputed: the historian Taddesse Tamrat argued it was Yetbarak, whose name was later struck from the records, while other accounts name Na'akueto La'ab. The Church's part is told in different ways. Later hagiographies credit the saint Tekle Haymanot with raising Yekuno Amlak and helping him to the throne; earlier ones give that role to Iyasus Mo'a, abbot of Istifanos. One tradition, reported by E. A. Wallis Budge, says the Zagwe king abdicated peacefully under a treaty arranged by Tekle Haymanot, receiving lands and royal honours in Lasta. Budge preferred another text, published by Carlo Conti Rossini, in which Yekuno Amlak won the throne in battle with soldiers raised through Tekle Haymanot and in return gave the Church a third of the kingdom.

Yekuno Amlak reigned until his death in 1285. He campaigned against the kingdom of Damot, intervened in the affairs of the Sultanate of Shewa, wrote to the Mamluk sultan Baybars asking for a new bishop from Egypt, and, according to Budge, exchanged letters and gifts with the Byzantine emperor. Budge calls his accession the point at which Ethiopian history, as distinct from legend, begins. His descendants ruled Ethiopia until 1974, when the last emperor, Haile Selassie, was overthrown in the Ethiopian Revolution, and the claim of descent from Solomon was written into the Ethiopian constitution of 1955. Modern historians regard that descent as a myth created to legitimise Yekuno Amlak's seizure of power.

Traditional history: imprisoned by the Zagwe king on Mount Malot, escaped, gathered support in Amhara and Shewa, with considerable aid from the Sultanate of Shewa defeated the Zagwe king at the Battle of Ansata (Wikipedia, Yekuno Amlak).
The dynasty was founded in 1270 (Wikipedia, Solomonic and Yekuno Amlak; Budge: accession in 1268 or 1270; restoration under Yekuno Amlak in 1270).

Taddesse Tamrat argued the last king was Yetbarak, removed from records; Getatchew Mekonnen Hasen names Na'akueto La'ab (Wikipedia, Yekuno Amlak; Budge: tradition names Na'akueto La'ab as the king who abdicated).
Later hagiographies say Tekle Haymanot raised him and helped depose the Zagwe; earlier ones credit Iyasus Mo'a, abbot of Istifanos (Wikipedia, Yekuno Amlak).
Budge, following Bruce: Takla Haymanot proposed that Na'akueto La'ab abdicate; a treaty gave him estates in Lasta and royal honours (attributed).

Budge: a text published by Conti Rossini says Yekuno Amlak, through Takla Haymanot, obtained soldiers, fought and conquered his adversary, and gave Takla Haymanot a third of the kingdom; Budge thinks this version correct (attributed).
Yekuno Amlak reigned 1270-1285 and died in 1285 (Wikipedia, Yekuno Amlak; Budge: reigned fifteen years).
He campaigned against Damot; a deposed ruler of the Sultanate of Shewa appealed to him in 1279; he wrote to Baibars for a new Abuna in 1273 (Wikipedia, Yekuno Amlak).
Budge states he exchanged letters with Michael VIII and sent giraffes (Wikipedia, Yekuno Amlak, citing Budge; attributed).
Budge: Abyssinian history only begins with the accession of Yekuno Amlak (attributed).

The dynasty ruled until 1974, when Haile Selassie was overthrown by the Derg in the 1974 revolution; the claimed descent was enshrined in the 1955 constitution (Wikipedia, Solomonic and Yekuno Amlak).

Marcus and Northrup: the Kebra Nagast descent is a myth/pastiche of legends to legitimise Yekuno Amlak's seizure of power (Wikipedia, Solomonic; Budge: Conti Rossini regards the dynasty as founded by Yekuno Amlak in the 13th century).

cp03-19.title: Kublai Khan proclaims the Yuan dynasty
paras: Kublai had been Great Khan of the Mongols since 1260, but after the civil war with his brother Ariq Boke his real power was limited to his own realm centred on China, while the western khanates went their own way. From the start of his reign he relied heavily on Chinese advisers and adopted Chinese models of government. He prepared to move the Mongol capital from Karakorum to China in 1264 and from 1266 built a new city near the old Jurchen capital Zhongdu, on the site of modern Beijing.

In 1271, the eighth year of his Zhiyuan era, Kublai issued an edict proclaiming the dynastic name Great Yuan (Da Yuan), in the manner of a traditional Chinese dynasty. The name comes from the Classic of Changes (I Ching), where it describes the origin of the universe or a primal force; H. H. Howorth's history translates it as 'original' or 'chief'. The edict claimed succession from earlier Chinese dynasties, back to the legendary Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors and through to the Tang. In Mongolian the state was called Dai Ön Ulus, often together with or replaced by 'Great Mongol State'. The following year Kublai made the new city, known to the Mongols as Khanbaliq, the capital, Dadu ('Great Capital'), while Shangdu remained his summer capital. Howorth adds that Kublai founded an academy for scholars and schools in the provinces and had Chinese classics translated into Mongolian.

The proclamation was a claim to rule all of China, much of which still belonged to the Southern Song. Kublai launched a massive offensive against the Song in 1274 and completed the conquest in 1279, when the last Song emperor died at the Battle of Yamen, making Kublai the first non-Han ruler of all of China proper. The Yuan dynasty ruled China until 1368, when the last Yuan emperor fled from Khanbaliq to Shangdu ahead of the armies of the Ming; his successors carried on the name Great Yuan in Mongolia as the Northern Yuan.

Q531916.title: First Mongol invasion of Burma
Q531916.place: Northern Burma and the Yunnan frontier
paras: After conquering the kingdom of Dali (Yunnan) in the 1250s, the Mongols bordered the Pagan Empire of Burma. In 1271-1272, as part of their drive to encircle the Song dynasty of China, they demanded tribute from King Narathihapate, and in 1273 Kublai Khan himself sent an embassy with the same demand. G. E. Harvey's History of Burma (1925) says the envoys were executed because they would not take off their shoes in the king's presence, against the advice of a minister who warned that earlier kings had never killed ambassadors. In 1275 Kublai ordered the Yunnan government to secure the borderlands and allowed it a limited frontier war if Pagan resisted.

In 1277 the Burmese attacked Kanngai, a small state on the Taping River whose chief had submitted to the Mongols, and were defeated by the Yunnan garrison at the battle the Burmese call Ngasaunggyan. Marco Polo, who described the battle, gives the Burmese 60,000 men and 2,000 elephants carrying wooden towers, and the Mongols 12,000 horsemen; the Yuan chronicle says 700 men beat a Burmese army of 40,000 to 50,000. In Polo's account the Mongol horses shied at the elephants, so the commander had his men dismount and shoot from the cover of the trees until the wounded elephants stampeded; Polo, as quoted by Harvey, names this commander Nasr al-Din, while Wikipedia calls him Huthukh and has Nasr al-Din lead a raid on Kaungsin late in 1277, which took the fort and then withdrew because of the heat.

In 1281 Kublai again demanded submission and, when Narathihapate refused, ordered the conquest of northern Burma, though not of Pagan itself. The invasion began on 22 September 1283. The Burmese fort at Ngasaunggyan fell on 3 December after a siege of over two months and Kaungsin six days later, with 10,000 Burmese losses according to the Mongol sources. The Mongols took the old capital Tagaung in February 1284 and, after a pause in the hot season, defeated another Burmese army near Hanlin in January 1285. Narathihapate panicked and fled to Lower Burma, which earned him the name Tarokpyemin, 'the king who fled from the Chinese'; Harvey says he had pulled down hundreds of pagodas to strengthen the capital's defences.

With his vassals in revolt, the king sued for peace. In June 1286 he sent an embassy led by the monk Shin Ditha Pamauk, and in January 1287 the envoys accepted Mongol overlordship and an annual tribute in Beijing in return for the withdrawal of Mongol troops. On 1 July 1287, however, Narathihapate was murdered by his son Thihathu. The Yunnan command then sent an army south under Kublai's grandson, named Ye-sin Timour in Wikipedia; older histories say it took Pagan, but recent research suggests it was held off by Burmese commanders well short of the capital and withdrew to Tagaung after heavy losses. The Pagan Empire, which had lasted some 250 years, broke apart, the Mongols kept northern Burma down to Tagaung as the province of Zhengmian, and Burma entered 250 years of political fragmentation in which Tai-Shan states rose across the region.

Q1369379.title: Battle of Bạch Đằng (1288)
Q1369379.place: Bạch Đằng River, Quảng Ninh, Vietnam
paras: In late 1287 Kublai Khan sent a third army against Đại Việt, the Vietnamese kingdom of the Trần dynasty, after his earlier invasion of 1285 had ended in a costly retreat. Prince Toghon (Thoát Hoan) led the land forces, while the admiral Omar (Ô Mã Nhi) commanded the fleet with Fan Yi (Phàn Tiếp). The Yuan took the capital Thăng Long (Hanoi) early in 1288, but King Trần Nhân Tông and the court escaped by sea; the Vietnamese commander-in-chief was Prince Trần Hưng Đạo (Trần Quốc Tuấn). The invaders depended on a supply fleet under Zhang Wenhu (Trương Văn Hổ). Prince Trần Khánh Dư ambushed it near Vân Đồn and destroyed or captured its grain ships, and Zhang escaped in a small boat.

Without supplies, and with the hot season coming, Toghon decided to withdraw: he would go overland towards Lạng Sơn while Omar's fleet returned by the Bạch Đằng River, the way it had come. Trần Hưng Đạo repeated the tactic Ngô Quyền had used on the same river against the Southern Han in 938. He had iron-tipped wooden stakes driven into the riverbed, according to Trần Trọng Kim's history Việt Nam sử lược by the general Nguyễn Khoái, and hid boats and troops along the banks. When the Yuan fleet came down the river at high tide, a small Vietnamese flotilla attacked and then fled, drawing the Yuan ships upstream past the stakes, hidden under the water.

As the tide went out, the Vietnamese turned back to fight, and Trần Hưng Đạo's main force joined them. The Yuan ships, trying to escape, ran onto the exposed stakes, where many were stuck, overturned or wrecked. The fighting lasted from sunrise to sunset; the Vietnamese took about 400 warships, and thousands of Yuan soldiers were killed or drowned. Wikipedia dates the battle to 9 April 1288; Trần Trọng Kim places it in the third lunar month of that year. Omar was captured. Wikipedia says Fan Yi was killed in the river, while Trần Trọng Kim says he too was captured and later died of illness in captivity.

Toghon's land army was ambushed on its retreat through the mountain passes and lost much of its strength before he escaped into China; Kublai banished him to Yangzhou. The victory ended Kublai's plans to conquer Đại Việt and Champa and is counted among the greatest in Vietnamese history. King Nhân Tông nevertheless sent envoys to the Yuan court offering tribute, and in 1289 he returned the prisoners; Omar's ship, by a plan of Trần Hưng Đạo, was sunk at sea on the way home. Relations remained strained until Kublai's successor Temür settled for a nominal tributary relationship.

cp03-22.title: Second Mongol invasion of Japan
paras: After the failure of his first invasion of Japan in 1274, Kublai Khan kept sending envoys to demand submission, and the Kamakura shogunate, led by the regent Hōjō Tokimune, had them beheaded in 1275 and again in 1279. The Japanese expected another attack. They organised the warriors of Kyūshū, built a stone wall along Hakata Bay, two metres high according to Wikipedia and some 20 km long according to the historian Kawai Atsushi, and drove stakes into likely landing places. Having completed the conquest of the Song in 1279, Kublai could now attack from two directions.

Two fleets set out in 1281. The Eastern Route army from Korea, of Mongol, Korean and northern Chinese troops, sailed first and attacked Tsushima and Iki in June; the much larger Southern Route fleet from southern China, many of its soldiers former Song troops, was delayed. The figures in the sources are large: Wikipedia gives 900 ships from Korea and 3,500 from southern China carrying 142,000 men, and Kawai 140,000 men, of whom 100,000 came from southern China. Modern historians think these numbers are exaggerated; estimates by Thomas Conlan and Morris Rossabi run from about 14,000 to about 70,000.

Without waiting for the southern fleet, the Eastern Route commanders attacked Hakata Bay and Nagato in late June. They could not get past the wall at Hakata, and the invaders occupied the islands of Shika and Noko. From there they were harried by Japanese night raids in small boats, in which warriors such as Kōno (Kawano) Michiari boarded and burned enemy ships, and the Mongols took to lashing their ships together for defence. When the southern fleet arrived, the combined force seized Taka Island off northern Hizen and pressed on towards Hakata, but some two months of fighting brought it no decisive gain.

Then a great typhoon struck the fleet at anchor: on 15 August 1281 according to Wikipedia, on 14-15 August according to James Murdoch's History of Japan, and on 23 August according to Kawai. Ships crowded at the mouth of Imari Bay were smashed against each other. Wikipedia reports a Chinese survivor's account that the commander Fan Wenhu sailed away in the best remaining ships, leaving the troops to their fate. The Japanese killed or captured the men stranded on Taka Island; the southern Chinese were spared and enslaved. A Korean source says 7,592 of the 26,989 Koreans who sailed did not return. The storm became known as the kamikaze, the 'divine wind', and fed the belief that Japan was protected by the gods. Murdoch writes that Kublai at once began planning a third expedition, but it was put off because Korea was exhausted and his ministers objected. In Japan the defensive war brought no conquered land with which the shogunate could reward its warriors, and its authority declined.

Q2672432.title: Mongol invasion of Java
paras: Kublai Khan sent envoys to many states of Southeast Asia demanding tribute. His envoy to Java, Meng Qi, was received with contempt by Kertanegara, king of Singhasari, who had his face branded like a common thief's and sent him home. In 1292 Kublai ordered a punitive expedition, which was also meant to bring the surrounding states and the sea trade routes under Yuan control. The History of Yuan records 20,000 to 30,000 men from southern China, 500 to 1,000 ships and provisions for a year; H. H. Howorth's history, following the Chinese annals, gives 1,000 ships and 30,000 soldiers. The commanders were Shi Bi, the Uyghur Yighmish and Gao Xing.

By the time the fleet arrived, early in 1293, Kertanegara was dead. In 1292, while much of his army was away in Sumatra, his vassal Jayakatwang of Kediri had rebelled, taken the capital and killed him. Kertanegara's son-in-law Raden Wijaya had submitted to Jayakatwang and been allowed to found a new settlement, Majapahit. When the Yuan forces landed, Wijaya offered to submit to the emperor and promised tribute if they helped him destroy Kediri. The allies defeated a Kediri army on the Kali Mas river and beat off an attack on Majapahit in April, and on 26 April they stormed Kediri's capital, Daha, after a battle lasting from morning to afternoon. Jayakatwang surrendered and was taken prisoner with his family.

Wijaya then turned on his allies. He went home, supposedly to prepare his tribute and the promised princesses, and asked for an unarmed escort; on 26 May his men ambushed the 200 Yuan soldiers sent with it and then attacked the main Yuan camp, driving the troops back to their ships. With the monsoon about to end, the Yuan forces withdrew, killing Jayakatwang and his son before they sailed on 31 May. The voyage home took 68 days. The losses of Shi Bi's troops were more than 3,000 men, the figure Howorth also gives, while a modern estimate cited by Wikipedia puts them far higher. They brought back prisoners, maps and loot.

In China Shi Bi was flogged and Shi Bi and Yighmish each lost a third of their property, though both were later pardoned, while Gao Xing was rewarded for saving the army from complete disaster. The expedition was the last of Kublai's reign; a further invasion planned with 100,000 men was cancelled after his death in 1294. Raden Wijaya's Majapahit became the most powerful state in the region.
