cp03-23.title: Death of Kublai Khan
paras: Kublai Khan, founder of the Yuan dynasty and Great Khan of the Mongols since 1260, had by the 1280s completed the conquest of the Song and ruled all of China, but his last years were overshadowed by losses. His favourite wife Chabi died in 1281, and his chosen heir, his son Zhenjin, died in 1286. His expeditions against Japan, Vietnam and Java had failed, and in the north he faced a long war with his cousin Kaidu. Kublai ate and drank heavily, grew very fat and suffered from gout; at the end of 1293 he refused to take part in the New Year ceremonies.

Before he died Kublai passed the seal of the crown prince to Zhenjin's son Temür. He died on 18 February 1294, aged 78; H. H. Howorth's history puts his death early in 1294, in the eightieth year of his age and the thirty-fifth of his reign. His body was taken to the burial place of the khans in Mongolia, and in the hall of ancestors he was given the temple name Shizu. Howorth notes that Chinese historians blamed him for favouring Tibetan lamas, for wasteful expeditions to Japan and Vietnam and for employing too many foreigners, while Mongol and Western writers judged his reign the most glorious in Mongol history.

At the assembly held after his death Temür was chosen over his brother Kamala; Howorth says Kublai's general Bayan stood sword in hand and declared he would accept no one but the heir the late khan had named. Temür ruled as Great Khan and second emperor of the Yuan. In name Kublai had headed the largest empire ever controlled by one man, but in practice the Mongol world had broken up after his war with Ariq Boke: the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate and the Ilkhanate were functionally independent states, and the Ogedeid Kaidu had been in revolt since 1269. Some of the western khanates still asked Kublai to confirm their new khans, and the Ilkhanate of Iran remained his close ally.

cp18-024.title: Tenochtitlan founded
paras: The Mexica were one of the peoples who, in their own migration stories, had come south from Aztlan, a legendary homeland in the north; their god Huitzilopochtli told them to part from the other tribes and take the name Mexica. When they reached the Valley of Mexico, which W. H. Prescott's History of the Conquest of Mexico (1843) dates to the early 13th century, the land was already held by city-states, the strongest being Culhuacan in the south and Azcapotzalco in the west. The Mexica moved from place to place: the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco drove them from Chapultepec, and in 1299 the ruler of Culhuacan let them settle on barren land at Tizapan, where they married into Culhua families, but in the end they were expelled again.

Their tradition told of a prophecy that they would find the site of their city where an eagle perched on a prickly-pear cactus, holding a snake. According to the legend they saw this sign on a small, swampy island near the western shore of Lake Texcoco, and there they founded Tenochtitlan. Prescott describes them sinking piles into the shallows and building huts of reeds and rushes, and living by fishing, hunting water birds and growing crops on chinampas, the so-called floating gardens. The date usually given is 1325, the year Prescott also accepts from the colonial-era historians Clavigero and Veytia, while Wikipedia notes that the exact date is unclear and that 13 March 1325 was chosen in 1925 for the city's 600th anniversary. The eagle on the cactus is still the emblem on the arms and flag of Mexico.

The early city was poor and divided; Prescott writes that a group of its people broke away to form a separate community on the neighbouring marshes, and Tlatelolco became a second Mexica city-state on the island. For about fifty years after their first king, Acamapichtli, was chosen in 1376, the Mexica were tributaries of Azcapotzalco and fought in its wars. Later they and their allies overthrew the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco, and the Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan grew into the Aztec Empire, with Tenochtitlan as its capital and the largest city of the pre-Columbian Americas until the Spanish and their Tlaxcalan allies took it in 1521.

cp18-093.title: Timur takes power
paras: Timur was born near Kesh (Shahrisabz), south of Samarkand, in the Chagatai Khanate. He belonged to the Barlas, a Turkicised Mongol tribe; Wikipedia describes his father Taraghai as a minor noble of the tribe, the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as its head. Later dynastic histories gave his birth as 8 April 1336, but most sources from his lifetime suggest the late 1320s. Wounds to his right leg and hand, received in about 1363, lamed him for life and gave him the Persian nickname Timur-i Lang, 'Timur the Lame', the origin of 'Tamerlane'. By about 1360 he was leading troops in Transoxiana, the land between the Oxus and the Jaxartes, which was then divided among quarrelling chiefs.

When Tughlugh Timur, the Chagatai khan of the east and a descendant of Genghis Khan, invaded Transoxiana, Timur was sent to negotiate with him and instead joined him, and was rewarded with the government of the country. After his father's death he also became head of the Barlas. Tughlugh later tried to set his own son Ilyas Khoja over Transoxiana, and Timur turned against him. Clements Markham's account of Timur's life, written for the Hakluyt Society's edition of Clavijo and following the Memoirs attributed to Timur, tells of a time as a fugitive in the deserts of Khwarazm with his brother-in-law, Amir Husayn, in 1362, when the two had only a handful of followers left; Timur's troops eventually drove the eastern Chagatai forces out.

The two allies then became rivals for Transoxiana. Wikipedia says Timur won over followers in Balkh, Husayn's base, with his generosity, while Husayn alienated people with heavy taxes. Around 1370 Husayn surrendered and was then killed; Markham writes that Timur gave way to his chiefs' demands, and that three chiefs dragged Husayn from a minaret where he had taken refuge. Timur was then formally proclaimed sovereign at Balkh, according to Markham by four revered descendants of the Prophet, and made Samarkand his capital. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places Husayn's death at the close of 1369, and Markham dates Timur's rule over Samarkand from 1369.

Because he did not descend from Genghis Khan, Timur could not take the title of khan. He married Husayn's widow Saray Mulk Khanum, a Chinggisid, and took the title güregen, 'royal son-in-law'; he called himself only amir and ruled in the name of a puppet khan, Suyurghatmish. He also styled himself Sahib Qiran, 'Lord of the Conjunction'. From Samarkand he spent the next thirty years in conquests that stretched from the Volga and Anatolia to Delhi.

cp18-094.title: Death of Timur
paras: By 1404 Timur had conquered an empire from Transoxiana across Iran to the Caucasus, sacked Delhi in 1398-1399, and in 1402 defeated and captured the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at Ankara. Back in Samarkand he held great festivities, at which the Castilian envoy Ruy González de Clavijo was present, and then turned against Ming China. Clements Markham, introducing Clavijo's narrative, says Timur was angered by an insolent message from Chinese envoys; Wikipedia says he detained a Ming envoy when he began the campaign in December 1404. Markham dates his departure from Samarkand to 8 January 1405, in heavy snow.

It was an unusual winter campaign for a commander who preferred to fight in spring. The army crossed the frozen Jaxartes (Syr Darya) and camped near Otrar, and there Timur fell ill with fever; Markham, who follows the traditional birth year of 1336, gives his age as sixty-nine. He died on 17 February 1405 according to Markham and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica; Wikipedia gives 17 or 18 February and places his death at Farab, near Otrar. His body was embalmed with musk and rose water, laid in an ebony coffin and taken to Samarkand, where his tomb, the Gur-e-Amir, still stands.

Timur had outlived both heirs he had named, his son Jahangir and his grandson Muhammad Sultan, and only on his deathbed did he choose Muhammad Sultan's brother Pir Muhammad. Pir Muhammad could not win enough support, and Timur's descendants fought one another for the succession; another grandson, Khalil Sultan, seized Samarkand, where Markham says he was crowned in March 1405. Timur's youngest son, Shah Rukh, ruler of Khorasan, overcame his rivals in 1409 according to Wikipedia (Markham says he was called to Samarkand in 1408) and ruled from Herat, but many provinces broke away and the Timurid state never regained Timur's extent. The Ming envoys detained by Timur were released, and the war against China was abandoned.

Q2888296.title: Conquest of Ceuta
paras: Ceuta, on the African shore of the Strait of Gibraltar, was a rich Marinid port, an outlet of the Saharan gold trade and a haven for Barbary corsairs, although by the 15th century it had declined and Morocco was weakened by civil war. King John I of Portugal planned to attack it in secret. C. R. Beazley's life of Prince Henry the Navigator says the idea came up when John's three eldest sons, Edward (Duarte), Peter and Henry, asked to be knighted, and the royal treasurer suggested a crusade in Africa in place of a year of tournaments. John sent an embassy to Sicily that stopped to spy out Ceuta's defences, and staged a quarrel with the Count of Holland so that Europe would think the fleet was meant for Holland. Queen Philippa died of plague just before the fleet sailed; according to Beazley she gave each of her sons a sword on her deathbed.

The fleet left Lisbon on 25 July 1415. Wikipedia counts about 200 ships carrying up to 50,000 men, about 19,295 of them soldiers, including English, French and German volunteers; Beazley gives 50,000 soldiers and 30,000 sailors. Only at Lagos was the target announced. Wikipedia describes how the governor, Salah ben Salah, gathered many tribesmen to defend the city when the first galleys appeared, but sent them home when storms scattered the Portuguese fleet and the attack seemed to have been abandoned.

The assault came on 21 August, the date Wikipedia gives; Beazley's account puts the fleet before Ceuta on the night of the 15th and the landing at the next dawn. Ruy Gonçalves was the first ashore, followed by Henry and Edward, who drove the defenders back through the gate of the landing place; resistance in the streets broke when a very large African warrior who had been hurling stones was killed. Henry and Peter were cut off in the town and for a time reported dead, but by evening the lower town was taken. That night Salah ben Salah abandoned the citadel, and when the Portuguese began to hack down its gates, two men left inside opened them. The flag of Lisbon was raised on the highest tower.

The main mosque was consecrated as a cathedral, and there the three princes were knighted in order of birth. The city was thoroughly plundered. Against the wishes of many of his men John decided to keep it, with Pedro de Meneses as governor and a garrison of 2,700 men. The capture is seen as the beginning of the Portuguese Empire, and Beazley argues that what Henry learned at Ceuta about the gold trade of the interior encouraged his voyages along the African coast. Wikipedia says Ceuta remained under Portuguese control until it was transferred to Spain in 1668; the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says it passed to Spain when Philip II took the Portuguese crown in 1580 and was definitively assigned to the Spanish crown by the treaty of Lisbon.

Q24945556.title: Siege of Angkor
paras: By the 14th century the Khmer Empire, ruled from Angkor since the period that began with the empire's founding in 802, faced the rising Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya, founded around 1350 on its western flank. Wikipedia, drawing on the Cambodian chronicles, describes earlier Siamese captures of Angkor in 1352 and 1393, each followed by a Khmer recovery. The historian Lawrence Palmer Briggs, in The Ancient Khmer Empire (1951), doubts this: in his view there had been much fighting in the border provinces, but Angkor itself was taken only once.

In 1430 King Borommarachathirat II of Ayutthaya invaded Cambodia and laid siege to Angkor Thom. Thai chronicle tradition says the siege lasted about seven months; the city was taken and plundered in 1431. According to Briggs, the Cambodian king Dharmasoka died during the siege, and two mandarins and two Buddhist monks went over to the besiegers. The Siamese carried off statues and many prisoners to Ayutthaya, and their king placed his own son on the Cambodian throne.

The Siamese did not stay to occupy the country. Briggs writes that the Khmer prince Ponhea Yat had the Siamese puppet killed and was crowned at Angkor, but found the old capital impossible to defend. Wikipedia says he fled the indefensible capital. Either way, he moved the court south-east to Basan (Srey Santhor) and then, according to Briggs in 1434, to Chaktomuk, the site of modern Phnom Penh at the junction of the Mekong and the Tonle Sap.

The move is conventionally taken as the end of the Angkor period and the start of the Post-Angkor period, though the temples of Angkor continued to be used for religious purposes. Historians debate how far the Siamese attack caused the decline: Briggs argued that the sack was a raid rather than a conquest and that Cambodia remained an independent and important state, while others point to the burden of maintaining the great monuments, the spread of Theravada Buddhism, or the breakdown of Angkor's water system as deeper causes.

cp18-061.title: Lê Lợi founds the Lê dynasty
paras: In 1407 Ming China conquered the short-lived Hồ state in what is now northern Vietnam and ruled it as the province of Jiaozhi. Ming rule, with its policy of assimilation, provoked a string of revolts. The one that succeeded began in early 1418 at Lam Sơn, a mountainous rural district of Thanh Hóa, where Lê Lợi, a wealthy landowner who had refused office under the Ming, raised an army and took the title Bình Định Vương (Pacifying King).

The first years went badly. Driven again and again into the Chí Linh mountains, the rebels were at one point reduced to eating vegetables and slaughtering their elephants and horses, and in 1423 Lê Lợi agreed a truce. From 1424 he struck south instead, took Nghệ An as a base and won control of most of the land from Thanh Hóa south to Thuận Hóa. In 1426 his armies moved north, and on 7 November 1426 they ambushed the Ming commander Wang Tong at Tốt Động and Chúc Động, near modern Hanoi. Wang Tong escaped wounded and was besieged in Đông Quan, the Ming seat of government. The Vietnamese chronicles claim more than 50,000 Ming dead in this battle; the historian Trần Trọng Kim, in his history Việt Nam sử lược, doubted the figure but accepted that it was a major defeat.

In 1427 the Xuande Emperor sent two relief armies, under Liu Sheng from Guangxi and Mu Sheng from Yunnan. Wikipedia gives them 110,000 men in all; Trần Trọng Kim gives Liu Sheng's column alone 100,000 men and 20,000 horses. Lê Lợi chose not to storm Đông Quan but to wait for the relief. Liu Sheng, pursuing a feigned retreat with some hundred horsemen, was ambushed and killed near the Chi Lăng pass; the rest of his army was destroyed at Xương Giang, and Mu Sheng withdrew. Wang Tong then made peace. At a ceremony south of Đông Quan on 16 December 1427 both sides swore an oath, and the Ming army began its march home on 29 December, Wang Tong himself following on 3 January 1428. Lê Lợi let the defeated troops go home and supplied them with boats and provisions.

During the war Lê Lợi had set up Trần Cảo, said to be a descendant of the old Trần kings, as a nominal ruler to satisfy the Ming. Early in 1428 Trần Cảo fled to Ngọc Ma, was caught and was made to drink poison; some historians think Lê Lợi arranged his death. On 29 April 1428 Lê Lợi took the throne, with the era name Thuận Thiên, restoring the country's name of Đại Việt. The scholar Nguyễn Trãi wrote the Bình Ngô đại cáo, a proclamation of victory and independence.

The Ming at first refused to recognise the new king and demanded a Trần heir; only after repeated assurances that the line had died out did the Xuande Emperor grant Lê Lợi a provisional title in 1431. Lê Lợi, known as Lê Thái Tổ, reigned until 1433. His dynasty became the longest-ruling in Vietnamese history, lasting until 1789 apart from the Mạc usurpation of 1527–1533.

cp18-025.title: Pachacuti begins the Inca expansion
paras: In the early 15th century the Incas were one of many small chiefdoms in the southern Andes, ruling a confederation that reached about 40 kilometres around Cusco. According to the Spanish chroniclers, their aged ruler Viracocha Inca had chosen as heir his son Inca Urco, passing over a younger son, Cusi Yupanqui, whom leading Inca captains favoured. The crisis came when the Chankas of Andahuaylas, a people thirty leagues west of Cusco, marched on the city.

In the account written by Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa in 1572 from the testimony of Inca nobles (and, historians note, partly to justify Spanish rule), Viracocha and Urco abandoned Cusco for a fortified refuge, while Cusi Yupanqui, then a youth of about 20, stayed with a handful of captains to defend it. The Chankas attacked the city from several sides and were driven back with heavy losses; later tradition said even the stones rose up to fight for the defenders. Cusi Yupanqui then defeated the Chankas a second time in the field, where their two war leaders were killed. When Viracocha wanted Urco to have the honour of treading on the captured spoils, the victor broke with his father, had himself crowned in Cusco's temple of the Sun and took the name Pachacuti, 'overturner of the world'. Urco died in a short civil war.

Pachacuti then turned Cusco's victory into an empire. He bound neighbouring chiefs to him through feasts, gifts and marriages, rebuilt Cusco and its temple of the Sun, and campaigned first against the Chankas' former allies and the peoples around Cusco, reaching the Soras some 40 leagues to the west. In the south he defeated and captured the Colla lord of the Lake Titicaca basin and occupied his seat at Hatun Colla. He moved loyal colonists (mitimaes) into unstable provinces, built roads, terraces and irrigation works, and is believed by most archaeologists to have had Machu Picchu built as an estate.

The date usually given, 1438, comes from the chronology that John Howland Rowe based on the chronicler Miguel Cabello de Balboa, in which Pachacuti reigned from 1438 to 1471. The Incas did not count years, and other reckonings differ: Philip Ainsworth Means placed his reign in 1400–1448, José Antonio del Busto put the defence of Cusco in 1424, and radiocarbon dates point to the early 15th century. Since the 1980s most scholars have treated the Chanka war itself as largely legendary. Pachacuti was succeeded by his son Tupac Inca Yupanqui, and within three generations the Inca realm spread over a large part of western South America.

cp18-096.title: Kazakh Khanate founded
paras: In the 15th century the descendants of Jochi, Genghis Khan's eldest son, fought for control of the nomads of the Dasht-i Qipchaq steppe, who were then known as Uzbeks. Abu'l-Khayr Khan of the Shibanid line, backed by the Manghit nobles, came out on top and also took over the Syr Darya lands of the rival line of Urus Khan. Two sons of Barak Khan, Urus Khan's grandson, Kerei (Girai) and Janibek, refused to accept his authority.

According to Mirza Muhammad Haidar Dughlat's Tarikh-i Rashidi, written in Kashmir around 1541–42, Kerei and Janibek, seeing that Abu'l-Khayr meant to remove Jochid princes he suspected of disloyalty, fled with a few other princes and their followers to Moghulistan. Its ruler, Esen Buqa (Isan Bugha) Khan, received them with honour and gave them land at Kozy Bashi near the Chu river, on the western edge of his realm. Living there as exiles on the frontier, after the practice called qazaqliq, in which defeated claimants withdrew to the margins and lived by hunting and raiding, they came to be known as Qazaq or Uzbek-Qazaq, a political label that later became the name of a people.

After Abu'l-Khayr's death his realm fell into strife, and many of his subjects joined Kerei and Janibek; the Tarikh-i Rashidi puts their following at about 200,000 people and says that the Kazakh sultans began to reign in 870 AH (1465–66), adding 'but God knows best'. That date, 1465, is the one generally accepted in Kazakh historiography. Russian historiography, following Tursun Sultanov, instead dates the khanate's formation to Abu'l-Khayr's death in 875 AH (1470–71).

Kerei was succeeded by his son Burunduk, and then by Janibek's son Kasym, under whom the Kazakhs came to dominate almost the whole steppe; Haidar Dughlat called him the most powerful ruler there since Jochi himself. The khanate later split into three hordes (zhuz) and lasted until the Russian Empire abolished the khans' office in 1822–1824.
